source_refs.note: Chapter 18 exercise (PDF 111-114), solved: 15 MCQs keyed from the chapter's text, 16 short (Q15 five problems worked step by step; Q16 ten pairs as tables), 14 long and 6 inquisitive questions. No answer key is printed. MCQ 1, 2, 6, 9, Short Q16 and Long Q1 carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: 1. In the monohybrid cross of Mendel, when a pure round-seeded plant was crossed with a winkled-seeded plant, all the F1 progeny were round-seeded, because of:
blocks.explanation: The round allele (R) is fully expressed in Rr and the wrinkled allele is not expressed at all, so F1 shows only the dominant trait: complete dominance (18.1, 18.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "winkled-seeded"; it should read "wrinkled-seeded".

blocks.prompt: 2. In a cross of AaBb x AaBb, what fraction of the offspring can be expected to express one of the two dominant alleles, but not both?
blocks.explanation: Dominant A only (A_bb) = 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; dominant B only (aaB_) = 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16. Total = 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16 (the 9:3:3:1 ratio: the two '3' classes).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) prints "9/1"; it is evidently meant to be 9/16 (the fraction showing both dominant traits). It is not the answer either way.

blocks.prompt: 3. In which of these cases, two genes can experience independent assortment?

options.text: They are located in close proximity on the same chromosome.
Crossing over between the genes does not occur.
They are located on different chromosomes or are far apart on the same chromosome.
The expression of one gene does not affect the expression of the other.

blocks.explanation: Genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same chromosome, assort independently; closely linked genes stay together (18.6.1).

blocks.prompt: 4. The blood group AB may be given to a person who has blood group;
blocks.explanation: AB blood has both antigen-A and antigen-B, so only a recipient without anti-A and anti-B antibodies, i.e. AB, can receive it (18.4.1).

blocks.prompt: 5. If father has blood group B and the mother has blood group A, what blood groups their children have?
blocks.explanation: If both parents are heterozygous (father Iᴮi, mother Iᴬi), the gametes Iᴮ, i × Iᴬ, i give IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴮi (B), Iᴬi (A) and ii (O): all four groups are possible.

blocks.prompt: 6. A gene for corn has two alleles, one for yellow kernels and one for white kernels. Cross pollination of yellow corn and white corn results in ears with approximately equal number of yellow and white kernels. Which term best describes the relationship between the two alleles?
blocks.explanation: Both the yellow and the white colour appear side by side in the ear, with no blending into an intermediate colour, so the book's intended term among the options is codominance (18.3.2); incomplete dominance would give an intermediate colour, and crossing over and recombination concern linked genes. See the Book correction: strictly, no option fits.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: No printed option fits exactly. Codominance means both alleles show in the same heterozygous individual (as in the MN blood group, 18.3.2). Here each kernel is a separate seed (offspring), and an ear with about equal numbers of yellow and white kernels is a 1 : 1 ratio, the result of a testcross such as Yy × yy with ordinary complete dominance. Crossing over (a) and recombination (b) concern linked genes, and incomplete dominance (c) would give an intermediate colour. (d) Codominance is keyed as the book's intended answer, because both parental colours appear side by side without blending.

blocks.prompt: 7. A cross between two plants with genotypes AaBb and AaBb results in an F1 generation that is 25% AABB, 50% AaBb, and 25% aabb. Which reason most likely explains why other possible genotypes are not present?

options.text: The loci of the genes are close together.
The loci of the genes are on different chromosomes.

blocks.explanation: Only parental combinations (AB and ab) appear, as in a 1:2:1 single-gene ratio, so A and B are completely linked: their loci are close together on the same chromosome and no crossing over separates them (18.6.1).

blocks.prompt: 8. In pea plants, the allele for tall stalks (T) is dominant over the allele for short stalks (t). Suppose a cross between a tall pea plant and a short pea plant produces 43 tall offspring and 47 short offspring. If one of the tall offspring is crossed with one of the short offspring, what ratio of genotypes would be most likely in their offspring?
blocks.explanation: 43 : 47 is about 1 : 1, so the tall parent was Tt (Tt × tt). A tall offspring is therefore Tt and a short one tt; Tt × tt again gives 1 Tt : 1 tt (testcross, 18.1).

blocks.prompt: 9. Allele B produces black coat colour while b produces white coat colour. Allele C produces curly fur while c produces straight fur. In a cross between two BbCc parents, predict the fraction of offspring with black coat colour and straight fur.
blocks.explanation: Worked out: black (B_) = 3/4; straight (cc) = 1/4; black and straight = 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16 (product rule, 18.2.2). The correct answer, 3/16, is not among the options. Option (b) 9/16 is the fraction for black and curly fur (B_C_), the answer the book most likely intended; see the Book correction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: None of the printed options is correct: black coat with straight fur (B_cc) is 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16. The printed fractions belong to other classes: 1/16 is white and straight (bbcc), 9/16 is black and curly (B_C_), 3/4 is all black offspring (B_), and 16/16 is the whole progeny. The key is set to (b) 9/16 only as the book's likely intended answer (the class with both dominant traits). In an exam, write 3/16 with the working.

blocks.prompt: 10. What is the criterion to mark an allele as dominant?

options.text: The frequency of the allele in population
The expression of the allele in heterozygous genotype
The location of the allele on chromosome
The frequency of the crossing over of the allele

blocks.explanation: An allele is dominant if it is expressed in the heterozygote (e.g. R in Rr) while the other allele is not; how common it is does not matter (18.1).

blocks.prompt: 11. Which of these characters is controlled by a multiple allelic system?
blocks.explanation: The ABO system is controlled by one gene (I) with three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i (18.3.3); in the chapter the Rh system has two alleles (D, d) and the MN system two alleles (Lᴹ, Lᴺ).

blocks.prompt: 12. Albinism is caused by a recessive gene. A woman with albino father marries an albino man. What will be the proportion of her progeny?
blocks.explanation: The woman is normal but received a recessive allele from her albino father (aa), so she is Aa. Aa × aa gives gametes A, a × a: 1 Aa (normal) : 1 aa (albino).

blocks.prompt: 13. When the activity of one gene is suppressed by the activity of a non-allelic gene, it is known as;
blocks.explanation: Epistasis is a non-allelic interaction in which an allele of one gene masks or modifies the effect of another gene at a different locus (18.5.2); the other options are allelic interactions.

blocks.prompt: 14. Which of the following is a result of Erythroblastosis fetalis?
blocks.explanation: Maternal anti-Rh antibodies destroy foetal RBCs: haemolytic anaemia; bilirubin from broken RBCs causes jaundice; high bilirubin can damage brain cells (18.4.3).

blocks.prompt: 15. Colour blindness is more common in males because it is a/an;
blocks.explanation: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive: a male shows it with one recessive allele on his single X, while a female needs two (18.8.1).

blocks.prompt: 1. Name the main exceptions to the Mendel’s laws of inheritance.
blocks.explanation:
1. Incomplete dominance and co-dominance (exceptions to the law of dominance).
2. Multiple alleles (more than two alleles).
3. Gene linkage and crossing over (exceptions to independent assortment).
4. Epistasis, polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy.
5. Sex-linked traits and environmental effects.

blocks.prompt: 2. What is probability? How does probability relate to genetics?
blocks.explanation:
Probability is how often a particular outcome occurs: number of times an event occurs ÷ total possible outcomes.
The transfer of genes to the next generation is random, so the chance of each allele combination in offspring is calculated by probability (product rule for independent events, sum rule for mutually exclusive events), e.g. Aa × Aa: aa = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

blocks.prompt: 3. Justify that multiple alleles provide many different phenotypes.
blocks.explanation: With only two alleles a gene gives at most three genotypes. With multiple alleles more combinations are possible: the ABO gene has three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i), giving six genotypes (IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi, IᴬIᴮ, ii). Because Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant and i is recessive, these give four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O). So multiple alleles increase variation.

blocks.prompt: 4. Name various human blood group systems.
blocks.explanation: The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognizes 43 human blood group systems. Main ones: ABO system, Rh system, MNS system, Lutheran, Kell, Lewis and Duffy systems.

blocks.prompt: 5. What do you mean by multiple alleles? Name the alleles responsible for ABO blood group system.
blocks.explanation:
Multiple alleles: a gene having more than two alternative forms (alleles) in a population, though each person carries only two of them.
ABO alleles: Iᴬ (makes antigen-A), Iᴮ (makes antigen-B) and i (makes no antigen) of gene I on chromosome 9.

blocks.prompt: 6. What is co-dominance. Give an example.
blocks.explanation:
Co-dominance: both alleles of a gene pair are fully expressed in the heterozygote, without blending or masking, so both parental phenotypes appear together.
Example: MN blood group; Lᴹ makes M antigen, Lᴺ makes N antigen, and LᴹLᴺ has both (MN group). Also Iᴬ and Iᴮ in the AB blood group.

blocks.prompt: 7. What antigens and antibodies are found in ABO blood group system?
blocks.explanation: Antigens on RBCs and antibodies in plasma (Landsteiner's rule: plasma has antibodies against the antigen that is absent):

blocks.prompt: 8. Justify why O-negative individuals are called universal donors and AB-positive individuals are called universal recipients.
blocks.explanation:
O-negative RBCs have no antigen-A, antigen-B or Rh-antigen, so no recipient's antibodies can attack them: universal donor.
AB-positive plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-Rh antibodies, so it does not attack any donor's RBCs: universal recipient.

blocks.prompt: 9. Why is human male referred as heterogametic?
blocks.explanation: Because his sex chromosomes are different (XY), so he produces two types of sperm: half carry an X chromosome and half a Y chromosome. The female (XX) produces only X-carrying eggs and is homogametic.

blocks.prompt: 10. What is gene linkage?
blocks.explanation: Gene linkage is the presence of genes on the same chromosome (linked genes); closely linked genes tend to be inherited together and do not assort independently during gamete formation, e.g. wing length and abdomen width in Drosophila.

blocks.prompt: 11. How can the linked gene assort independently?
blocks.explanation: By crossing over in meiosis-I: chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments, so linked alleles are separated and recombinant gametes form. Genes far apart on the same chromosome cross over so often that they assort almost independently.

blocks.prompt: 12. List at least five polygenic traits in humans.
blocks.explanation:
1. Height
2. Skin colour
3. Weight
4. Intelligence
5. Eye colour (beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: 13. Write brief note on Y-linked inheritance in humans.
blocks.explanation: Y-linked (holandric) genes lie only on the non-homologous region of the Y chromosome and have no alleles on X. Their traits appear only in males and pass from father to all sons. They are rare because Y has few genes. Examples: hypertrichosis (hair on the rim of pinna), porcupine man, webbing of toes.

blocks.prompt: 14. Define sex linkage and give an example.
blocks.explanation:
Sex linkage: inheritance of traits controlled by alleles present on sex chromosomes (usually the X, since Y carries almost no functional genes), so their ratio differs in males and females.
Example: red-green colour blindness or haemophilia (X-linked recessive), more common in males.

blocks.prompt:
15. Solve the following genetic problems:
i. A plant of genotype AABbCC is self-pollinated. Calculate the phenotypic ratio of F2 generation.
blocks.explanation:
Parents: AABbCC × AABbCC
Genes AA and CC are homozygous, so only Bb segregates.
Gametes: ABC and AbC from each parent.
Offspring: 1 AABBCC : 2 AABbCC : 1 AAbbCC
Phenotypes: AABBCC and AABbCC show the dominant B trait; AAbbCC shows recessive b.
Phenotypic ratio = 3 : 1

blocks.prompt:
15. Solve the following genetic problems:
ii. In four-o’clock plant, the red and white flower colours show incomplete dominance. Calculate the ratios in crosses between (i) two red-flowered plants; (ii) a red-flowered and a pink-flowered plant; (iii) a pink-flowered and a white-flowered.
blocks.explanation:
Alleles: R (red), W (white); RR = red, RW = pink, WW = white.
(i) Red × red: RR × RR; gametes R × R; offspring all RR: all red.
(ii) Red × pink: RR × RW; gametes R × R, W; offspring 1 RR : 1 RW: 1 red : 1 pink.
(iii) Pink × white: RW × WW; gametes R, W × W; offspring 1 RW : 1 WW: 1 pink : 1 white.

blocks.prompt:
15. Solve the following genetic problems:
iii. A man with blood group A marries a woman who has blood group AB. What blood groups are expected among their children?
blocks.explanation:
Woman AB = IᴬIᴮ; gametes Iᴬ, Iᴮ.
Man A may be IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi.
Case 1: IᴬIᴬ × IᴬIᴮ → IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴮ: blood groups A and AB (1 : 1).
Case 2: Iᴬi × IᴬIᴮ → IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi: A : AB : B = 2 : 1 : 1.
So the children can have A, AB or B; never O.

blocks.prompt:
15. Solve the following genetic problems:
iv. Two white sheep produce a black offspring. What are the parents’ genotypes for the colour? What is the probability that their next offspring will be black?
blocks.explanation:
A black lamb from two white parents means white is dominant (W) and black recessive (w); the black lamb is ww, so each parent gave one w.
Parents' genotypes: Ww × Ww (both heterozygous).
Gametes: W, w × W, w.
Offspring: 1 WW : 2 Ww : 1 ww (3 white : 1 black).
Probability of a black next offspring = 1/4 (25%).

blocks.prompt:
15. Solve the following genetic problems:
v. Albinism (lack of pigment) in man is caused by a recessive gene. If normal parents have an albino child, what is the probability that their next child will be normal for colour?
blocks.explanation:
The albino child is aa, so each normal parent carries a: parents Aa × Aa.
Gametes: A, a × A, a.
Offspring: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (3 normal : 1 albino).
Probability that the next child is normal = 3/4 (75%).

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Gene and allele
blocks.explanation: A gene can have different forms called alleles.

rows: A sequence of nucleotides of DNA that codes for a polypeptide; unit of a character
An alternative form of a gene, giving an alternative trait
Occupies a specific locus on a chromosome
Alleles occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Genotype and phenotype
blocks.explanation: The genotype is the blueprint and the phenotype is the visible outcome.

rows: Combination of alleles in an individual
Not visible; found by crosses (e.g. testcross)

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Homozygous and heterozygous
blocks.explanation: Both describe the gene pair of an individual.

rows: Both alleles of the gene pair are similar
Formed by fusion of gametes with the same allele
Formed by fusion of gametes with different alleles
Not pure-breeding; two types of gametes

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Monohybrid and dihybrid cross
blocks.explanation: They differ in the number of characters studied together.

rows: Inheritance of one character (one gene pair)
Inheritance of two characters together (two gene pairs)
Example: RrYy × RrYy (seed shape and colour)
Basis of law of independent assortment

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Incomplete dominance and co-dominance
blocks.explanation: In both, neither allele masks the other in the heterozygote.

rows: Both alleles fully express their effects
Heterozygote shows both parental phenotypes at a time
Example: MN and AB blood groups

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Epistasis and polygenic inheritance
blocks.explanation: Both involve more than one gene, but they work differently.

rows: An allele of one gene masks or modifies the effect of another gene
Many genes add their small effects to one trait
Example: wheat grain colour, human skin colour, height

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• XX-XY and ZZ-ZW sex determination
blocks.explanation: Both are chromosomal systems; the heterogametic sex differs.

rows: Male is heterogametic (X and Y sperms)
Female is heterogametic (Z and W eggs)

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• XX-XY and XX-ZO sex determination
blocks.explanation: In both the female is XX; the male differs.

rows: Male XY: has a Y chromosome
Male XO: no Y, only one X
Male and female have equal chromosome numbers
Male has one chromosome less (grasshopper: male 23, female 24)
Sperms carry X or no sex chromosome (nullo gamete)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The pair prints "XX-ZO sex determination"; it should read "XX-XO" (the system of grasshoppers, in which the male has one X and no Y).

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Sex-linked and sex-limited traits
blocks.explanation: Both differ in ratio in males and females, for different reasons.

rows: Genes on autosomes, present in both sexes
Expressed in both sexes, but in different ratios
Expressed in only one sex (anatomy or hormones)
Example: beard in men, milk production in females, horns in male sheep

blocks.prompt:
16. Differentiate between:
• Sex-limited and sex-influenced traits
blocks.explanation: Both are autosomal traits whose expression depends on sex.

rows: Due to anatomical or hormonal differences
Allele dominant in one sex, recessive in the other (hormonal)
Example: beard, milk production, ovarian cancer
Example: baldness, amount of body hair

blocks.prompt: 1. Explain Mendel’s experiment which led to the formulation of the law independent assortment.
blocks.explanation:
Mendel studied two characters of pea together: seed shape (round R dominant, wrinkled r recessive) and seed colour (yellow Y dominant, green y recessive).
P: pure-breeding round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy).
Gametes: RY × ry.
F1: all RrYy, round and yellow (dihybrids).
F1 self-fertilized: each F1 plant forms four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY, ry. 4 male × 4 female gametes give 16 combinations.
F2 phenotypes: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.
Each pair still gave 3 : 1 (12 round : 4 wrinkled; 12 yellow : 4 green), so seed shape was inherited independently of seed colour, and new combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) appeared.
Law of independent assortment: 'each pair of alleles assorts independently of other pairs of alleles during gamete formation.' Modern form: genes on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis, because homologous pairs line up randomly.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "the law independent assortment"; it should read "the law of independent assortment".

blocks.prompt: 2. Explain incomplete dominance and exemplify it through the inheritance of flower colour in 4 O’ clock plant.
blocks.explanation:
Incomplete dominance: neither allele is fully dominant; the heterozygote shows a phenotype intermediate between the two parents (the effects blend).
Example, Japanese four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa):
P: red (RR) × white (WW)
Gametes: R × W
F1: all RW, pink flowers (neither red nor white).
F1 × F1: RW × RW; gametes R, W × R, W.
F2: 1 RR (red) : 2 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white).
Here the genotypic and phenotypic ratios are the same (1 : 2 : 1), unlike Mendel's 3 : 1, because the heterozygote can be recognised. The alleles do not blend permanently: red and white reappear in F2.

blocks.prompt: 3. Explain Erythroblastosis foetalis in the light of antigen-antibody reaction. What measures can be taken to prevent Erythroblastosis foetalis?
blocks.explanation:
Erythroblastosis foetalis is a haemolytic disease of the foetus/new-born caused by Rh incompatibility.
Antigen-antibody reaction:
1. It occurs when an Rh-negative mother (dd) carries an Rh-positive foetus (Dd), the D allele coming from an Rh-positive father.
2. Foetal blood (with Rh-antigen) may enter the mother's blood, especially at delivery. Rh-negative people have no natural anti-Rh antibodies, so the mother's immune system is sensitized and makes anti-Rh antibodies, which stay for life.
3. Usually the first baby escapes, but in a later Rh-positive pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta into the foetal blood and react with the Rh-antigen on foetal RBCs, destroying them.
Complications: haemolytic anaemia; enlarged liver and spleen (trying to make more RBCs); bilirubin from broken RBCs causes jaundice and can damage brain cells; miscarriage or stillbirth in severe cases.
Prevention and treatment:
1. Rh-antiserum (anti-Rh antibodies) injected into the Rh-negative mother during early pregnancy and immediately after birth; it destroys any foetal RBCs in her blood before they sensitize her immune system.
2. Testing the Rh group of the mother (and father) early, so at-risk pregnancies are known.
3. The affected new-born's blood is replaced by Rh-negative blood free of anti-Rh antibodies.
4. ABO incompatibility (e.g. O-negative mother, A- or B-positive baby) naturally protects, because her anti-A or anti-B destroy entering foetal RBCs first.

blocks.prompt: 4. Describe polygenic inheritance, using an example from grain colour in wheat.
blocks.explanation:
Polygenic inheritance: a character controlled by many gene pairs whose alleles add their effects (additive); the combined effect gives one trait with continuous variation, e.g. height, skin colour, weight, intelligence.
Wheat grain colour (white to dark red) is controlled by three polygenes A, B, C. Each dominant allele (A, B, C) adds red pigment; recessive alleles (a, b, c) add none. Colour depends on the number of dominant alleles.
P: dark red (AABBCC) × white (aabbcc)
F1: AaBbCc, intermediate red.
F1 × F1: each parent forms 8 kinds of gametes, giving 64 combinations in F2.
F2: 1 dark red (6 dominant alleles) : 6 : 15 : 20 (intermediate, 3 dominant) : 15 : 6 : 1 white (0 dominant). Only one in 64 is darkest red (AABBCC) and one white (aabbcc); the other 62 show shades of red.
The many classes form a continuous range (bell-shaped curve); environment (light, water, nutrients) also affects colour.

blocks.prompt: 5. Explain epistasis with the help of an example.
blocks.explanation:
Epistasis is a non-allelic gene interaction in which an allele of one gene masks or modifies the effect of alleles of another gene at a different locus. The masking allele is epistatic; the masked one is hypostatic. It changes the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio.
Example, coat colour in Labrador dogs (two genes):
1. Gene B controls pigment colour: B (black) dominant over b (brown).
2. Gene E controls deposition of pigment in fur: E allows deposition; ee blocks it, so the coat is yellow whatever B or b is present (e is epistatic to B/b).
Cross: two heterozygous black dogs BbEe × BbEe.
F: 9 B_E_ black : 3 bbE_ brown : 3 B_ee yellow + 1 bbee yellow = 4 yellow.
Ratio 9 : 3 : 4 instead of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Other examples: flower colour in foxglove (dominant W limits pigment to spots, so DdWw selfed gives 12 white : 3 dark red : 1 light red); Bombay phenotype (hh prevents A and B antigens, so the person types as O).

blocks.prompt: 6. Explain how gene linkage counters independent assortment and crossing-over modifies the progeny.
blocks.explanation:
Gene linkage counters independent assortment:
1. Thousands of genes lie on a limited number of chromosomes (humans about 20,000 genes on 23 pairs), so many genes lie in a line on each chromosome.
2. Genes on the same chromosome (linked genes) tend to be inherited together; they do not assort independently. So a dihybrid does not form its four kinds of gametes in equal numbers; parental combinations are more frequent.
3. Detection: if a cross shows parental and new combinations in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, genes are not linked; if parental combinations are more and new ones fewer, linkage is incomplete; if only parental combinations appear, linkage is complete (e.g. Morgan's Drosophila, F2 3 : 1 instead of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1).
Crossing over modifies the progeny:
1. In meiosis-I, chromatids of homologous chromosomes line up and exchange segments; DNA strands break and re-join.
2. The genes stay in the same order, but the alleles are rearranged, so linked alleles are separated.
3. Recombinant chromatids go to different gametes, producing new combinations (recombinants) in the progeny, beside the parental types.
4. So crossing over breaks linkage, makes incomplete linkage, and is a source of genetic variability; genes far apart cross over more often and behave almost independently.

blocks.prompt: 7. Exemplify the concept of gene linkage by quoting the example of wing length and width of abdomen in Drosophila melanogaster.
blocks.explanation:
Thomas Hunt Morgan studied two traits in Drosophila: wing length (long L dominant over vestigial l) and abdomen width (broad B dominant over narrow b).
P: long wings, broad abdomen (LLBB) × vestigial wings, narrow abdomen (llbb).
F1: all long wings, broad abdomen (LlBb, with L and B on one chromosome and l and b on its homologue).
F1 × F1: by independent assortment, F2 should be 9 long-broad : 3 long-narrow : 3 vestigial-broad : 1 vestigial-narrow (the 3 : 3 classes being new combinations).
Observed F2: only parental combinations, 3/4 long wings-broad abdomen and 1/4 vestigial wings-narrow abdomen; no new combinations.
Conclusion: the genes for wing length and abdomen width lie close together on the same chromosome and do not assort independently; each F1 forms only LB and lb gametes, giving 3 : 1 like a single gene. This is complete linkage.

blocks.prompt: 8. Explain the XX-XY mechanism of sex determination in Drosophila and mammals.
blocks.explanation:
In Drosophila, mammals and most other vertebrates, sex is determined by the sex chromosome pair: a rod-shaped X and a hook-shaped Y.
Karyotype: Drosophila has 3 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (female 6 + XX, male 6 + XY); humans have 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (female 44 + XX, male 44 + XY).
Mechanism:
1. The female (XX) is homogametic: all eggs carry one X.
2. The male (XY) is heterogametic: half the sperms carry X and half carry Y.
3. X-sperm + egg → XX zygote → female; Y-sperm + egg → XY zygote → male.
4. So the sperm decides the sex, and males and females are produced in a 1 : 1 ratio.
In humans, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome makes a protein that starts development of testes and prevents female structures.

blocks.prompt: 9. Describe the XX-XO and ZZ-ZW sex determination systems and evaluate by studying the karyotype.
blocks.explanation:
Karyotype is the number, size and shape of the complete set of chromosomes; all pairs are alike in both sexes except the sex chromosomes.
1. XX-XO system (some insects, e.g. grasshopper):
Karyotype: 22 autosomes (11 pairs) in both sexes. Female has XX: 24 chromosomes. Male has only one X and no Y (XO): 23 chromosomes.
Gametes: all eggs carry X; the male forms two types of sperm, half with X and half with no sex chromosome (nullo gamete).
X-sperm + egg → XX female; nullo sperm + egg → XO male. The male is heterogametic and the sperm decides the sex.
2. ZZ-ZW system (birds):
Karyotype: the autosome number varies among birds; females have ZW and males ZZ.
Gametes: the female is heterogametic, forming half Z eggs and half W eggs; all sperms carry Z.
Z-egg + sperm → ZZ male; W-egg + sperm → ZW female. Here the egg decides the sex.
Evaluation by karyotype: in the XX-XO system the sexes differ in chromosome number (24 vs 23); in the ZZ-ZW system the number is the same, but the female's sex pair is unequal (Z and W) while the male's is alike (ZZ).

blocks.prompt: 10. Explain the inheritance of a sex-linked trait in Drosophila.
blocks.explanation:
In 1910, T. H. Morgan found a white-eyed male Drosophila among normal red-eyed flies. Let Xᴿ = red (dominant) and Xʳ = white (recessive), on the X chromosome; Y has no allele.
1. White-eyed male (XʳY) × red-eyed female (XᴿXᴿ) → F1 all red-eyed (XᴿXʳ females, XᴿY males): red is dominant.
2. F1 × F1 (XᴿXʳ × XᴿY) → F2 about 3 red : 1 white, but all white-eyed flies were males (XʳY); females were XᴿXᴿ or XᴿXʳ, all red.
3. Testcross F1 red female (XᴿXʳ) × white male (XʳY) → red females, white females, red males, white males in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, so white-eyed females can exist.
4. White-eyed female (XʳXʳ) × red-eyed male (XᴿY) → all females red (XᴿXʳ), all males white (XʳY) (criss-cross inheritance).
Conclusion: the eye-colour gene lies on the X chromosome and the Y has no allele for it; such genes and traits are sex-linked. A male shows a recessive X-linked trait with one allele, and gets his X from his mother.

blocks.prompt: 11. Describe sex-influenced and sex-limited traits with common examples from human genetics.
blocks.explanation:
Both are autosomal traits (their genes are not on sex chromosomes) whose ratio differs in males and females.
1. Sex-limited traits: the genes are present in both sexes but expressed in only one, due to anatomical or hormonal differences. Examples: growth of beard in men; milk production in females; prostate cancer only in males and ovarian cancer only in females. (In animals: horns in male sheep.) Sex-limited genes are responsible for sexual dimorphism.
2. Sex-influenced traits: the same gene is expressed in both sexes but differently; the allele is dominant in one sex and recessive in the other, due to hormonal differences. Examples: baldness and the amount of body hair. The baldness allele is dominant in men and recessive in women: a man is bald with one or two baldness alleles (homozygous or heterozygous), while a woman is bald only if she has two baldness alleles. So baldness is much more common in men.

blocks.prompt: 12. Write a note on the inheritance of haemophilia in humans.
blocks.explanation:
Haemophilia is a rare disorder in which blood fails to clot properly after injury, due to reduction, malfunction or absence of clotting factors. Types:
1. Haemophilia A: abnormal factor VIII; X-linked recessive.
2. Haemophilia B: abnormal factor IX; X-linked recessive.
3. Haemophilia C: abnormal factor XI; autosomal recessive, equal in both sexes.
Inheritance of A and B (Xᴴ = normal, Xʰ = haemophilia):
1. A male with one Xʰ is haemophiliac (XʰY), since Y has no allele; a female must be XʰXʰ, so it is far more common in males. A heterozygous female (XᴴXʰ) is a normal carrier.
2. Carrier mother × normal father (XᴴXʰ × XᴴY): daughters 1/2 normal, 1/2 carriers; sons 1/2 normal, 1/2 haemophiliac.
3. Haemophiliac father × normal mother (XᴴXᴴ × XʰY): all daughters carriers, all sons normal (a son does not get his father's X).
4. Two normal parents can have a haemophiliac son only if the mother is a carrier.

blocks.prompt: 13. Write a note on the inheritance of colour blindness in humans.
blocks.explanation:
Normal (trichromatic) vision uses three kinds of cones in the retina: red-, green- and blue-sensitive, each with its own pigment protein (opsin). The genes for red and green opsins are on the X chromosome; the blue opsin gene is on autosome 7. Recessive opsin alleles cause colour blindness:
1. Dichromacy: two colours seen, the third missing: red-blindness (protanopia), green-blindness (deuteranopia), blue-blindness (tritanopia).
2. Monochromacy (total colour blindness): only one colour seen; rare.
Inheritance of red-green colour blindness (X-linked recessive; Xᴺ = normal, Xⁿ = colour-blind):
1. A male with one Xⁿ is colour-blind (XⁿY); a female must be XⁿXⁿ, so it is more common in males. XᴺXⁿ females are carriers with normal vision.
2. Carrier mother × normal father: 1/2 of sons colour-blind; 1/2 of daughters carriers.
3. Colour-blind father × normal mother: all daughters carriers, all sons normal.
4. Colour-blind mother: all her sons are colour-blind.
There is no cure; colour-blind glasses, special software and colour-discrimination training help.

blocks.prompt: 14. Explain Morgan’s experiment to explain crossing over and gene linkage.
blocks.explanation:
Gene linkage (Morgan's experiment): Morgan crossed Drosophila with long wings and broad abdomen (LLBB) with flies having vestigial wings and narrow abdomen (llbb). F1 were all long-broad (LlBb). F1 × F1 should give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 by independent assortment, but only parental combinations appeared, 3 long-broad : 1 vestigial-narrow. He concluded that the two genes lie on the same chromosome and are inherited together (linkage); L and B on one homologue, l and b on the other.
Crossing over: during meiosis-I, the chromatids of homologous chromosomes line up and exchange segments; DNA strands break and re-join. If crossing over happens between two linked genes (e.g. between L and B), the alleles are rearranged into new combinations (Lb and lB), so recombinant offspring (long wings-narrow abdomen, vestigial wings-broad abdomen) appear in small numbers beside the parental types (incomplete linkage). The fewer the recombinants, the closer the genes (beyond the chapter: recombination frequency is used to map genes). Thus linkage keeps genes together, and crossing over breaks linkage and creates variation.

blocks.prompt: 1. Collect data from the class or the college to see how many individuals have AB blood group and construct a pie chart and histogram for the collected data.
blocks.explanation:
This is an activity; the answer is your own data. Method:
1. Ask each student their ABO and Rh blood group (from a blood test or card) and record it in a tally table: A, B, AB, O (and positive/negative).
2. Count the total and each group; percentage of a group = (number in group ÷ total) × 100.
3. Pie chart: angle of each sector = (number in group ÷ total) × 360°; draw sectors for A, B, AB and O, label them with percentages.
4. Histogram (bar graph): blood groups on the x-axis and number of students on the y-axis; draw a bar for each group.
5. Conclude: AB is usually the smallest group, because it needs both Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles together, while the recessive i allele is common.

blocks.prompt: 2. Use a dice to calculate how many times out of 100 throws can you get sixes.
blocks.explanation:
Probability of a six in one throw = 1 (one face) ÷ 6 (possible outcomes) = 1/6.
Expected sixes in 100 throws = 100 × 1/6 ≈ 16.7, i.e. about 17.
Throw the dice 100 times and record the sixes; the actual count will be close to 17 but will vary, and comes nearer to 1/6 as the number of throws increases. In the same way, genetic ratios (3 : 1, 1 : 1) are probabilities, seen clearly only in large numbers of offspring.

blocks.prompt: 3. Derive an idea to get alternatives of blood transfusion. (reference could be made to synthesized plasma and serum).
blocks.explanation:
(Beyond the chapter.) Blood is needed to restore volume, carry oxygen and clot. Alternatives:
1. Plasma substitutes (volume expanders): saline, Ringer's solution, albumin, dextran or synthetic colloid solutions restore blood volume and pressure after blood loss; synthesized plasma and serum proteins (e.g. albumin, clotting factor concentrates such as factor VIII for haemophiliacs) replace particular components.
2. Artificial oxygen carriers: haemoglobin-based solutions and perfluorocarbons that carry oxygen without RBCs and need no ABO/Rh matching.
3. Stimulating the patient's own blood formation: erythropoietin, iron and vitamin supplements.
4. Using the patient's own blood: storing it before planned surgery (autologous transfusion) and cell salvage of blood lost during surgery.
5. RBCs grown in the laboratory from stem cells (under research).
Such alternatives avoid matching problems, transfusion reactions and infection.

blocks.prompt: 4. Justify why a recessive blood group allele of ‘i’ is more frequent in population.
blocks.explanation:
The allele i is passed on by every blood group except AB, and it is hidden in carriers (Iᴬi, Iᴮi), so it is not lost:
1. O (ii) × O (ii): all children O (ii).
2. Iᴬi × Iᴬi: 25% children O (ii).
3. Iᴮi × Iᴮi: 25% children O (ii).
4. Iᴬi × Iᴮi: 25% children O (ii).
In this way the i allele keeps reappearing in every generation, so it is the most frequent ABO allele and O is a common blood group.

blocks.prompt: 5. Justify blood donation as a service to suffering humanity.
blocks.explanation:
1. Blood cannot be manufactured; patients depend on donors.
2. Donated blood saves lives in accidents, surgery, childbirth with heavy bleeding, and anaemia.
3. Patients of thalassaemia and haemophilia need blood or blood products regularly; Rh-negative blood is needed for new-borns with erythroblastosis foetalis.
4. One donation can be separated into RBCs, plasma and platelets and help several patients; O-negative blood (universal donor) is valuable in emergencies.
5. It is safe for a healthy donor; the body soon replaces the blood (beyond the chapter). It costs the donor little but gives life to another, so it is a true service to humanity.

blocks.prompt: 6. Suggest ways to save lives through the knowledge gained in this chapter.
blocks.explanation:
1. Blood transfusion: match ABO and Rh groups of donor and recipient to prevent agglutination; use O-negative in emergencies.
2. Prevent erythroblastosis foetalis: test the Rh group of mothers; give Rh-antiserum to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and after birth; exchange transfusion for affected babies.
3. Genetic counselling for families with haemophilia, colour blindness, muscular dystrophy, albinism: predict risks from pedigrees and Punnett squares; identify carriers.
4. Embryonic screening (ultrasound, chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis) to detect genetic disorders and abnormal chromosome numbers early.
5. Early care of genetic disorders: clotting factor treatment for haemophilia, physical therapy and medicines for muscular dystrophy.
6. Avoiding marriages between close relatives reduces recessive disorders (beyond the chapter).
7. Regular voluntary blood donation.
